parts.note: reads as someone who makes dishonest dealing, but means a maker of sharp things: knives and blades

explanation.surface: A firm known for cheating its customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sharp practice' is an idiom for dishonest dealing; here it is taken literally, as the work of someone who makes things with sharp edges.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutler is a tradesman who makes and sells knives and other bladed tools.

clue.text: It may look wavy on the weather map but is nothing to the fighting sailor

definitions.text: It may look wavy on the weather map

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
RM stands for Royal Marine, a soldier who serves at sea

explanation.surface: A forecaster's wiggly line means little to a marine at war.
explanation.walkthrough: RM (Royal Marines) is the British corps of sea-going soldiers, hence 'fighting sailor'. 'to' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An isotherm is a line on a weather chart joining places of equal temperature, usually drawn as a curve.

clue.text: Proof that a death has been contrived with little prompting

indicators.note: something contrived has been artfully arranged, so these letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Evidence that a killing was staged, as in a detective story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has been contrived' rearranges all fifteen letters of PROOF THAT A DEATH; the murder-mystery surface hides that the fodder is the clue's opening words.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means instantly and willingly, needing hardly any persuasion or signal.

clue.text: Not a lively looker but useful for extending shrouds

explanation.surface: An unexciting watcher who nonetheless helps with the rigging.
explanation.walkthrough: Shrouds here are a ship's rigging ropes, not burial cloths; a deadeye is the wooden block through which a lanyard tensions them.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifeless gaze is a dead eye; on a sailing ship a deadeye is a round wooden block used to tighten the shroud ropes.

explanation.surface: Messing about in the manner of a light-headed farm animal.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy is a billy goat, a male goat; a dizzy one would be a giddy goat.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to behave foolishly; read literally it describes a light-headed male goat.

clue.text: Writing the text of the play

explanation.surface: Composing the words an actor will speak.
explanation.definitionFit: Script means handwriting or lettering, and also the written words of a drama or film.

clue.text: Detectives may be looking for a hint about K's follower

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for hint goes round the letter

parts.note: a hint or prompt is a cue
L follows K in the alphabet

explanation.surface: Sleuths searching for a suggestion about whoever comes after K.
explanation.definitionFit: Detectives hunt for evidence and pointers that help solve a crime.

clue.text: Kills the goose with out further discussion

definitions.text: Kills the goose with out further discussion

parts.words: Kills the goose with out further discussion
parts.note: silencing a goose ends its noisy chatter, which is taken as stopping idle talk and getting on with things

explanation.surface: A farmer dispatches a bird without debate.
explanation.walkthrough: A goose's cry is a cackle, so killing the goose silences the cackle; the phrase means to stop chattering and get down to business. The paper prints 'with out' as two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to stop the idle talk and get straight to the point.

clue.text: … to keep a hold on the nest-egg?

explanation.surface: Gripping tightly onto one's savings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nest-egg' suggests savings, but here it is literal: eggs in a nest.
explanation.definitionFit: To clutch is to grip tightly; a clutch is also a set of eggs laid in a nest at one time.

explanation.surface: A thorough account of the nursery-rhyme shepherdess's sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, Little Bo-Peep's sheep come home with their tails left behind them, so they are de-tailed.
explanation.definitionFit: Detailed means thorough and full; read as de-tailed it describes sheep that have lost their tails.

explanation.surface: A small coin's motion, and a generous one at that.
explanation.walkthrough: William Penn was a Quaker, and Quakers are the Society of Friends, so a 'Penn-y' movement is a Friendly one; 'Penny' is not the coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A Quaker (Friend) action, as Penn was one; and also any kindly sign or act of goodwill.

clue.text: Old Sussex port that could be made into a sort of whisky

explanation.surface: A historic harbour town that might be distilled into a spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: Rye in East Sussex was one of the Cinque Ports, England's old defensive harbours, and is now inland.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye is a former port town in East Sussex; rye is also a whiskey distilled from that grain.

parts.note: afoot suggests a plot is brewing, but literally means a thing worn on a climber's foot

explanation.surface: Climbers suspect a plot is under way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something afoot' usually means a scheme is in progress; here it is a thing literally on the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A crampon is a spiked metal plate strapped to a climbing boot for grip on ice.

clue.text: Find this classic character in your Homer

indicators.note: in tells you the answer sits within the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: An invitation to look for a figure from antiquity in your copy of the Iliad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to letters across 'youR HOmer'; the surface wants a hero from Homer's epics, but the 'character' is a Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rho is the seventeenth letter of the Greek alphabet, a character of the classical language.

parts.note: seems to ask how many pupils leave each year, but asks the age in years at which they leave

explanation.surface: A statistic on how many pupils finish school each year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annual number' looks like a yearly head count; it is a number of years, the age at which British pupils could leave secondary school.
explanation.definitionFit: The minimum school-leaving age in Britain was this many years when the puzzle appeared.

clue.text: A trio have to work assiduously when the board is somewhat thin

parts.note: a trio is a group of three
to ply is to work steadily at a task, as in plying a trade

explanation.surface: Three people must work hard when the plank they stand on is flimsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have to' and 'when the board is' only link; the board is plywood made of three layers, fairly thin.
explanation.definitionFit: Board made of three layers of wood glued together is fairly slim compared with thicker plywood.

indicators.note: the way things changed signals that the word before is rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone recounts how events turned out differently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Related' looks like the verb 'told', but its seven letters are rearranged; 'the way things' signals the shuffle and 'changed' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Something altered has been modified or made different.

parts.note: reads as a held-back retaliation, but means a regulated cost asked at a shop counter

explanation.surface: A measured military counter-attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counter charge' suggests a counter-attack; split it as a charge made over a shop counter, with 'restrained' meaning held down by regulation.
explanation.definitionFit: A price fixed or capped by authority is one kept in check, a regulated cost for goods.

explanation.surface: A warning to mind your cardiac health.
explanation.definitionFit: Ticker is slang both for a wristwatch and for the heart, each beating out a rhythm.

clue.text: Taken in by ungentlemanly type, some lady exchanged for money

indicators.note: taken in by means held inside, so the woman's word goes within the cad

parts.note: a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably
some lady is a female person, she

explanation.surface: A woman is fooled by a scoundrel and swapped for cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' reads as deceived, but here it means placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheque or token is cashed when it is turned into banknotes or coins.

clue.text: … and the leverage you might get with it

explanation.surface: Continuing from the money clue: the grip you gain by having it.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening ellipsis ties 'it' to the previous clue's money, so what you get with it is a bought item.
explanation.definitionFit: Purchase means a firm grip giving mechanical advantage, and also something bought.

clue.text: Group of soldiers taken aback by chief's retinue

indicators.note: taken aback suggests surprise but means turned back, so the run is read backwards
by tells you the letters come from within the words beside it

explanation.surface: Troops startled by a leader's entourage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken aback' reverses the run TINU found in 'reTINUe'; the surprise reading of 'taken aback' is the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a military body such as a platoon or company.

parts.note: someone easy is readily talked round

explanation.surface: A smooth-talking Greek who is soon won over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oily' looks like a description of the man's manner, but it is the plain definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Greasy means covered in or full of fat, slick like grease.

indicators.note: way-out means wild or unconventional, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone arrives through the exit to view a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'way-out' rearranges the six letters of IN CAME; 'picture shower' is a place that shows pictures, not a rain of images.
explanation.definitionFit: A movie theatre is where films, or pictures, are screened to an audience.

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the central letters are rearranged
the heart of a word is its central letters

explanation.surface: The most courageous person has had their heart shattered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart' takes AVE from the middle of 'brAVEst', and 'broken' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eva is a female given name, standing for any woman.

explanation.surface: The leftover sediment belonging to a US commander.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general of the American Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: General Robert E. Lee's possessive is spelt the same as lees, the sediment left in a wine cask.
